title: AI Literacy: Using AI Wisely, Safely and Critically
subtitle: Use AI chatbots to save real time at work, check every answer like a professional, and lead others to use AI responsibly.
description: A practical course on how today's AI tools work, where they help and where they mislead. You will set up tools safely on your phone, follow a reliable prompt-to-final workflow, fact-check AI output, and then help a team or organisation adopt AI with a clear policy.
outcomes: Explain how a large language model produces answers and why it hallucinates
Decide, task by task, where AI is safe and useful using a reliability and risk grid
Set up AI tools with privacy protections and anonymise data before use
Produce finished work with a prompt, draft, check, edit workflow and a check record
Detect and correct false facts, wrong arithmetic and bias in AI output
Run discovery, cost support and write a one-page AI use policy for a team
audience: Women professionals, entrepreneurs and community leaders who already use a smartphone and want to use AI with confidence and good judgement, and help others do the same.
tools: A free account on one AI chatbot (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude or Copilot)
Google Drive or similar for your portfolio

modules.title: How AI Works and Where It Fits
modules.overview: You will learn what today's AI tools really are, how a chatbot builds an answer one piece at a time, and why that explains both its strengths and its mistakes. You will finish the module able to judge, task by task, where AI can safely help in your own work and community.

lessons.title: What today's AI can and cannot do: a reality check
objectives: Distinguish predictive AI from generative AI using everyday examples
List tasks current AI chatbots do well and tasks where they often fail
Place any task on a reliability and risk grid before deciding to use AI
Explain why a confident AI answer is not the same as a correct one

blocks.text: **Artificial intelligence (AI)** is a broad name for computer systems that do tasks we normally link with human thinking: recognising speech, sorting information, translating, predicting and writing. You have probably used AI for years without calling it that. The spam filter in Gmail, the word suggestions on your phone keyboard, the fastest-route advice in Google Maps and the face unlock on many phones are all AI.

Since late 2022 a newer kind has become popular: **generative AI**. Instead of only sorting or predicting, it produces new text, images, audio or video when you type a request. The best known are chatbots such as **ChatGPT** (OpenAI), **Gemini** (Google), **Claude** (Anthropic), **Microsoft Copilot** and **Meta AI**, which appears inside WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook in some countries.

blocks.name: artificial-intelligence
blocks.alt: A person standing beside a large AI symbol on a screen
blocks.caption: Generative AI tools are new, but AI itself has been on your phone for years.

blocks.text: Two families of AI

head: Type
What it does
Everyday example
rows: Learns patterns from past data to sort, score or forecast
Spam filter, fraud alert from your bank, traffic estimate on a map
Produces new content in answer to a request (a prompt)
A chatbot drafting a letter, an app turning a photo into a cartoon, an AI voice reading text aloud

blocks.text: This course is mainly about generative AI, because that is what most people now use directly. But the same lesson applies to both: AI learns from patterns in data. It does not understand the world the way a person does, and it does not know when it is wrong unless it has been built to check.
What chatbots are genuinely good at

items: **First drafts**: letters, reports, lesson notes, meeting agendas, job descriptions.
**Rewriting**: making text shorter, simpler, more formal or friendlier.
**Summarising** a long document you paste in, so you know where to read closely.
**Explaining** a concept in simple words, then again with an example.
**Brainstorming**: twenty ideas for a workshop title, of which you keep three.
**Structuring**: turning messy notes into a table, checklist or outline.

blocks.text: Where they often fail

items: **Facts, figures and recent events**: they can invent names, dates, laws, prices and quotes. This is called a **hallucination**.
**Sources**: they may cite books, articles or web links that do not exist.
**Arithmetic** in long calculations, especially when numbers are written inside sentences.
**Local detail**: Nigerian procedures, fees, place names and languages such as Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo and Pidgin are often handled less accurately than English or American topics.
**Judgement about people**: decisions on hiring, health, credit or discipline need a responsible human, not a chatbot.

blocks.title: Confident is not correct
blocks.text: A chatbot writes a wrong answer in the same calm, fluent tone as a right one. Fluency is what it is built for. Accuracy is something you must check.
A simple test before you use AI

Ask two questions about any task. First: **how reliable is AI for this kind of task?** Drafting and rewriting are high; precise facts and local rules are low. Second: **how much harm would a mistake cause?** A wrong word in a birthday message is low harm. A wrong dosage, fee, legal deadline or bank detail is high harm. Put the two answers together and you know how to proceed.

blocks.title: Reliability and risk grid
items: Use freely, light check
Use, then check every fact
Use with care, human decides
Avoid or use expert source
axes: AI reliability for the task (high to low)
blocks.caption: Top left is where AI saves most time safely; bottom right is where you go to the original source or a qualified person.

blocks.title: Worked example: sorting a week of tasks
blocks.context: For example, Amaka coordinates a women's cooperative in Owerri. On Monday she lists five tasks and places each one on the grid before opening any AI tool.
steps: Thank-you message to volunteers after a market day: high reliability, low harm. She lets AI draft it and edits the names herself.
Summary of a 12-page training report for the committee: high reliability, medium harm. She uses AI, then checks every number against the report.
Current CAC fee to register the cooperative as an incorporated trustee: low reliability, high harm. She goes to the CAC website and calls the office instead.
Advice to a member about her child's fever: health, high harm. She does not use a chatbot; she refers the member to a clinic.
Ten ideas for a savings drive slogan: high reliability, low harm. She uses AI and picks two to discuss with members.
blocks.result: Three of five tasks get AI help, one gets AI help with careful checking, and two go to official or professional sources. She saves time without trusting AI where it is weak.

blocks.title: AI is a tool, not an authority
blocks.text: Treat a chatbot like a fast, well-read assistant who sometimes makes things up. You stay responsible for anything you send, sign or share.

Keep this grid in mind for the rest of the course. Every later lesson, from prompting to fact-checking to writing a team AI policy, builds on the same idea: match the amount of checking to the amount of harm a mistake could cause.

takeaways: Predictive AI sorts and forecasts; generative AI produces new content from a prompt.
Chatbots are strong at drafting, rewriting, summarising and brainstorming.
They are weak at exact facts, sources, long arithmetic and local Nigerian detail.
Decide by two questions: how reliable is AI here, and how bad is a mistake?

activity.title: Map your own week on the grid
steps: Write down eight real tasks from your work, business or community role this week.
For each task, mark AI reliability as high, medium or low using the lists in this lesson.
Mark the harm if wrong as low, medium or high.
Place each task in one of the four boxes of the grid and write the action: use freely, use then check, human decides, or avoid.
Circle the two tasks where AI could save you the most time safely.
activity.evidence: A photo or screenshot of your completed grid with eight tasks and the action for each

lessons.title: How a chatbot builds an answer: tokens, training and hallucinations
objectives: Describe in plain words how a large language model produces text
Use key terms correctly: prompt, token, context window, training data, knowledge cutoff
Estimate the token size of a document using the 4 characters rule
Explain why hallucinations happen and what reduces them

blocks.text: Chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude run on a **large language model**, usually shortened to **LLM**. An LLM is a very large computer program that has been trained on a huge amount of text from books, websites and other sources. During training it learned one main skill: given some text, **predict what comes next**.

When you type a question, the model does not look up a stored answer. It reads your words and predicts the next small piece of text, adds it, then predicts the next piece, and so on, until the answer is complete. This is why answers appear on screen word by word. It is also why the model can produce a sentence that sounds right but is false: it is choosing likely words, not checking facts.

blocks.name: ai-response
blocks.alt: A chat window showing an AI reply being produced
blocks.caption: Each reply is built piece by piece, by predicting the most likely next piece of text.

blocks.title: From your prompt to its answer
items: You type a prompt
Text split into tokens
Model predicts next token
Token added, repeat
Answer shown to you
blocks.caption: The model loops through prediction many times; nothing in this loop checks the answer against reality.

blocks.text: The words you need

head: Term
Plain meaning
rows: What you type or say to the AI: your question, instruction and any text you paste in
A small piece of text the model works with, often part of a word. Short common words are one token; long or unusual words are split into several
How much text the model can hold in mind at once, counting your prompt, any pasted document and its reply
The large collection of text the model learned from before it was released
The date after which the model learned nothing new in training. Unless the tool searches the web, it may not know recent events
A confident answer that is false or made up, such as a fake law, statistic or reference
A model that can take or produce more than text: photos, voice, documents
A feature where the tool searches the internet and shows links; useful, but you must still open the links

blocks.text: Counting tokens

OpenAI's own guidance gives a rule of thumb for English: **one token is about 4 characters**, and **100 tokens is about 75 words**. Other languages, including Yoruba, Hausa and Igbo with their tone marks, usually need more tokens for the same meaning. Tokens matter because free plans and context windows have limits, and paid developer tools charge by the token.

blocks.title: Worked example: will my report fit?
blocks.context: For example, Zainab wants a chatbot to summarise a 3,000-word project report for her NGO. She wants to know roughly how many tokens it will use.
steps: Rule: 100 tokens is about 75 words, so 1 word is about 100 / 75 = 1.33 tokens.
Report: 3,000 words x 1.33 = about 4,000 tokens.
Her instruction prompt is about 60 words, so 60 x 1.33 = about 80 tokens.
She asks for a 300-word summary: 300 x 1.33 = about 400 tokens.
Total for the exchange: 4,000 + 80 + 400 = about 4,480 tokens.
blocks.result: About 4,500 tokens is well inside the context window of the main chatbots today, so the whole report fits. A 300-page book would not fit in many free plans, and she would need to work chapter by chapter.

blocks.text: Why hallucinations happen

A model fills gaps with plausible text. If you ask for "three studies on market women in Kano" and its training data has little on that topic, it may still produce three neat titles with authors and years, because that is what such an answer usually looks like. The titles can be entirely invented. The same happens with phone numbers, fees, section numbers of laws and quotations from famous people.

items: **Gaps in training data**: less text about a topic means more guessing. Local Nigerian topics are often thin.
**Knowledge cutoff**: anything that changed after training, such as a new fee or policy, is unknown to the model.
**Pressure to answer**: models are trained to be helpful, so they tend to give an answer rather than say "I don't know".
**Long chats**: in very long conversations, early details can be lost or mixed up.

blocks.text: What reduces hallucinations

items: Give the source yourself: paste the document and say "answer only from the text below".
Ask the model to say "not stated in the text" if the answer is missing.
Use a tool with web search for current facts, then open and read the links it shows.
Ask for exact quotes from your pasted text so you can find them and confirm.
Keep chats focused; start a new chat for a new task.

blocks.title: Ask it to show where
blocks.text: When a chatbot summarises your document, ask: "For each point, quote the sentence it came from." If it cannot quote it, treat the point as unreliable.

Once you see a chatbot as a very skilled next-word predictor, its behaviour makes sense. It is brilliant with language and structure, and unreliable with facts it was never given. The rest of this course is about using the first strength while guarding against the second.

takeaways: An LLM predicts the next token again and again; it does not look up a stored answer.
About 4 characters, or three quarters of a word, make one English token.
Hallucinations come from gaps, cutoffs and the pressure to always answer.
Pasting your own source and asking for quotes cuts errors sharply.

activity.title: Catch a hallucination on purpose
steps: Open any free chatbot and ask: "List three published studies about women traders in my town, with authors and years." Use your own town.
Copy the answer into your notes.
Search for each title in Google Scholar or Google. Record whether each one really exists.
Now paste a short real article or report you have and ask the same tool to answer only from that text, quoting its sources.
Compare the two answers and write three sentences on the difference.
activity.evidence: Your notes showing the three claimed studies, what your search found for each, and your three-sentence comparison

lessons.title: AI in Nigeria and Africa: real uses, language gaps and opportunities
objectives: Name the main African and Nigerian AI policy documents and what they aim to do
Explain why AI tools work less well in many African languages
Calculate the realistic time saving from AI on a repeated work task
Identify two responsible AI opportunities in your own setting

blocks.text: AI is not only a Silicon Valley story. Governments, universities and businesses across Africa are shaping how it is used here. As an AI-literate professional you should know the main frameworks, the real gaps, and where practical value is for people like you and the women you serve.

blocks.name: connected-world
blocks.alt: People connected across a world map
blocks.caption: African policy makers and communities are actively shaping how AI is used on the continent.

blocks.text: The policy picture

head: Document
Who and when
What it is for
rows: African Union, endorsed by the AU Executive Council in July 2024
An Africa-centred, development-focused approach to AI that promotes ethical, responsible and fair use across member states
Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Nigeria, August 2024
Nigeria's plan for building AI skills, infrastructure and responsible use; released as a draft for input
Enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)
Rules on collecting and using personal data, which apply when you put people's details into any digital tool, AI included
Recommendation on the Ethics of AI
UNESCO, adopted by member states in November 2021
Global principles such as human oversight, fairness, transparency and protecting privacy

blocks.text: You do not need to memorise these. What matters is the shared message: AI should serve people, protect their data, avoid unfair treatment and stay under human control. Those principles will shape the AI use policy you write in Module 3.
The language gap

Most chatbots learned mainly from English text on the internet. Far less written material exists online in Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo, Pidgin and hundreds of other African languages. The result: translations and answers in these languages can be stiff, wrong in tone marks, or simply mistaken. Groups such as **Masakhane**, a grassroots research community for African language technology, work to close this gap, but you should still have a fluent speaker check anything important before it goes to members.

blocks.title: Check translations before sharing
blocks.text: If you use AI to translate a health notice, savings rule or meeting decision into Hausa or Igbo, ask a fluent speaker to read it before you send it. A wrong word can change the meaning completely.
Where AI is genuinely useful here

items: **Office and programme work**: drafting reports, minutes, letters and training handouts.
**Learning**: explaining a hard topic in simple words, making practice questions, planning study time.
**Small business**: product descriptions, customer replies, simple price lists, ideas for stock displays.
**Community leadership**: turning long notes into clear announcements, preparing agendas and checklists.
**Accessibility**: reading text aloud, turning voice notes into text, making large-print versions.

blocks.text: Counting the real time saving
A common mistake is to count only the time AI saves in writing and forget the time needed to check. Always add the checking time back in.

blocks.title: Monthly report with and without AI
items: Without AI
With AI and checking
blocks.caption: AI shortens drafting, but checking takes longer, so the true saving is smaller than it first looks.

blocks.title: Worked example: is it worth it?
blocks.context: For example, Hadiza is a programme officer in Kaduna who writes four field reports a month, as in the comparison above.
steps: Time per report without AI: 30 + 90 + 20 = 140 minutes.
Time per report with AI: 30 + 25 + 35 = 90 minutes.
Saving per report: 140 - 90 = 50 minutes.
Saving per month: 50 x 4 = 200 minutes, which is 3 hours 20 minutes.
Saving per year: 200 x 12 = 2,400 minutes, which is 40 hours.
blocks.result: Hadiza gains about 40 working hours a year, roughly five full working days, from one task, while still checking every fact. That is a real, honest case for AI, not a hopeful guess.

blocks.text: Notice what made the saving trustworthy: she measured her own times, included checking, and kept a human responsible for the final report. When you later advise a team or client, use the same method instead of quoting general promises about AI.

blocks.title: Data and cost on a phone
blocks.text: Typing text to a chatbot uses little mobile data compared with voice chat, image creation or video. If data is costly, prefer typed prompts, and download long reports on Wi-Fi.
Questions to ask about any new AI app

New apps often advertise themselves as "AI made for Africa" or promise to answer any question in your language. Some are excellent; some are copies built to collect data. Before you or your members rely on one, ask:

items: Who made it? Is there a real company name, website and contact address?
Is it in the official Google Play Store or Apple App Store, with a privacy policy you can read?
Where does your data go, and can you delete your account and chats?
Does it ask for permissions it does not need, such as your contacts or SMS?
Does it ask for payment or bank details before you have even tried it?

blocks.text: If you cannot answer these questions clearly, use one of the well-known tools from Lesson 2.1 instead.
Opportunities for you

AI-literate women can become the trusted person who helps others use these tools safely: training cooperative members, helping a school set rules for staff, or supporting an NGO to save time on reporting. Modules 2 and 3 give you the workflow, checking habits and leadership tools to do this well.

takeaways: The AU strategy, Nigeria's draft AI strategy, the NDPA 2023 and UNESCO's recommendation share one message: AI must serve people under human control.
Chatbots are weaker in African languages; a fluent speaker must check translations.
Count true time saved by adding checking time back in.
Your opportunity is to be the trusted, careful AI helper in your community or workplace.

activity.title: Measure one task honestly
steps: Pick one written task you do at least twice a month.
Next time, time yourself doing it the usual way, in minutes, for each stage.
The time after, use a chatbot for the draft and time each stage, including checking.
Calculate the saving per task, per month and per year as in the example.
Write one sentence on whether the quality was better, the same or worse.
activity.evidence: A small table of your timings for both methods, your monthly and yearly saving, and your quality note

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of predictive AI rather than generative AI?
options: A chatbot writing a thank-you letter
Your bank flagging an unusual card payment as possible fraud
An app turning your photo into a cartoon
A tool reading your text aloud in a new voice
quiz.explain: Fraud alerts score a payment against past patterns, which is prediction. The other three produce new content.

quiz.q: Amaka needs the current CAC registration fee for her cooperative. Where should she get it?
options: Ask a chatbot and use its answer
Ask two different chatbots and take the average
The official CAC website or office
A WhatsApp broadcast forwarded by a friend
quiz.explain: Fees change and chatbots often get local figures wrong. A high-harm, low-reliability fact must come from the official source.

quiz.q: Using the rule that 100 tokens is about 75 words, roughly how many tokens is a 1,500-word document?
options: About 1,125
About 1,500
About 2,000
About 6,000
quiz.explain: 1,500 x 100 / 75 = 2,000 tokens. (6,000 would be using 4 tokens per word, which mixes up the characters rule.)

quiz.q: Why can a chatbot list research papers that do not exist?
options: It is programmed to deceive users
It predicts text that looks like a typical answer, even when it lacks the facts
It copies fake papers from the internet on purpose
It only happens when the internet connection is slow
quiz.explain: The model generates likely-looking text. With gaps in its data it can produce realistic but invented titles: a hallucination.

quiz.q: Without AI a task takes 120 minutes. With AI drafting it takes 40 minutes plus 30 minutes of checking. How much time does AI save on each task?
options: 80 minutes
50 minutes
30 minutes
90 minutes
quiz.explain: With AI: 40 + 30 = 70 minutes. Saving: 120 - 70 = 50 minutes. Forgetting the checking time gives the wrong answer of 80.

modules.title: Tools, Workflow and Checking
modules.overview: You will choose and set up AI tools safely on your phone, follow a repeatable workflow from task to finished work, and check AI output for false facts, bad arithmetic and bias. By the end you will keep a simple check record that shows exactly what you verified and changed.

lessons.title: Choosing and setting up AI tools safely on your phone
objectives: Compare the main free AI chatbots and pick one for a given need
Change privacy settings so your chats are not used for training where the tool allows it
Secure your AI accounts with a strong password and two-step verification
Decide what information must never be pasted into a chatbot

blocks.text: You do not need a laptop or a paid plan to use AI well. All the main chatbots have free versions that run in a phone browser or app. What matters more than which tool you pick is how you set it up and what you put into it.

blocks.name: chat-with-ai
blocks.alt: A woman chatting with an AI assistant on her phone
blocks.caption: A phone and a free account are enough to start, if the account is set up safely.

blocks.text: The main tools

head: Tool
Made by
Useful to know
rows: Free plan with limits; app and web; can read uploaded files and photos
Works with your Google account; can link to Gmail, Docs and Drive if you allow it
Strong with long documents and careful writing; free plan with daily limits
Free with a Microsoft account; built into Edge and Windows
Appears inside WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook in some countries; convenient but mixes with personal chats

blocks.text: Paid plans for the main chatbots have commonly been priced at around **US$20 a month** (approximate, check the current price in the app). Paid plans give higher limits and newer models. For most learners in this course the free plans are enough. If you do pay with a naira card, check the final naira amount on your bank statement, because exchange rates and card charges change.

blocks.title: Try two, keep one
blocks.text: Run the same three real tasks through two tools and compare the results. Keep the one that gives you the clearest answers for your kind of work, and learn it well.
Privacy settings to change on day one
Most chatbots may use your conversations to improve their models unless you turn this off. The names of settings change, but these were the main controls at the time of writing:

items: **ChatGPT**: Settings, then Data Controls, then switch off "Improve the model for everyone". Use **Temporary Chat** for anything you do not want saved in your history.
**Gemini**: open your Google account's Gemini Apps Activity and choose whether activity is kept, and for how long.
**Claude and Copilot**: open the privacy or data section of settings and read what is collected and what you can switch off.
**All tools**: delete old chats you no longer need.

blocks.title: Never paste these into any chatbot
blocks.text: BVN, NIN, bank account and card numbers, passwords and one-time codes; members' or clients' phone numbers, addresses, health details or photos without their permission; confidential contracts or donor documents. Under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, you are responsible for how you handle other people's personal data.
Protect the account itself

items: Use a long, unique password, for example three random words with numbers, that you do not use anywhere else.
Turn on two-step verification in the tool or in the Google or Microsoft account you sign in with.
Sign out on shared or borrowed phones and never save the password there.
Download apps only from the Google Play Store or Apple App Store, from the real developer. Fake "AI" apps are a common way to steal data and money.

blocks.title: Safe setup checklist
items: Official app or website
Strong password, two-step on
Training on your chats off
Temporary chat for sensitive work
No ID, bank or client data
blocks.caption: Five checks to finish before you use any AI tool for real work.

blocks.text: Removing personal details before you paste

Often you need AI help with a document that contains personal data. The safe habit is to **anonymise** it first: replace names with roles or letters, remove phone numbers and addresses, and round exact amounts if they are not needed.

blocks.title: Worked example: anonymising a complaint before asking for help
blocks.context: For example, Blessing manages a small savings group in Ibadan. A member has sent a long, angry voice note that Blessing has typed up. She wants AI help to write a calm reply.
steps: Original line: "Mrs Funmilayo Adeyemi, 0803 000 0000, of 12 Oke-Ado Road, says her 45,000 naira contribution was not recorded."
She replaces the name with "Member A", deletes the phone number and address, and keeps the amount because it matters to the reply.
Anonymised line: "Member A says her 45,000 naira contribution was not recorded."
She opens a Temporary Chat and asks: "Write a calm, respectful reply to a savings group member who says her contribution was not recorded. We are checking the records and will respond within 3 days."
She pastes the draft into WhatsApp, adds the member's name herself, and checks the 3-day promise is realistic before sending.
blocks.result: The chatbot never sees the member's name, phone number or address, yet Blessing still gets a good draft in two minutes.

blocks.title: AI voice and video scams
blocks.text: Criminals now use AI to copy voices and faces. If a call or voice note from a "relative" or "boss" asks for urgent money or codes, hang up and call them back on the number you already have, or ask a question only the real person would know.
With a sensible tool, safe settings and a no-paste list, you are ready to use AI for real work. The next lesson gives you a workflow so the results are reliable every time.

takeaways: Free plans of ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude or Copilot are enough to start.
Turn off model training on your chats where offered and use temporary chats for sensitive work.
Never paste ID numbers, bank details, passwords or other people's personal data.
Anonymise documents before asking AI for help with them.

activity.title: Set up one tool safely
steps: Choose one chatbot and install it from the official app store or open the official website.
Set a unique password and turn on two-step verification.
Find the data or privacy settings and switch off training on your chats if the option exists.
Write your personal no-paste list of at least six items, and save it in your phone notes.
Anonymise one real message or document using the method in the worked example.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your privacy setting and two-step verification screen (hide any personal details), your no-paste list, and a before-and-after of the anonymised text

lessons.title: From task to finished work: the prompt, draft, check, edit workflow
objectives: Write a clear prompt using role, task, context, format and limits
Improve a weak first answer with follow-up prompts
Follow a five-stage workflow that keeps you in control of the final result
Choose when to stop prompting and finish the work yourself

blocks.text: Most disappointing AI results come from vague prompts. "Write a report" gives the model almost nothing, so it fills the gaps with generic text. A good prompt gives it the same information you would give a new assistant on her first day.

blocks.name: ai-generated-document
blocks.alt: A document being produced with AI help
blocks.caption: A clear prompt turns a generic draft into one that fits your real task.

blocks.text: Five parts of a clear prompt

head: Part
Question it answers
Example
rows: Who should the AI act as?
"Act as an experienced adult literacy trainer."
"Write a one-page handout explaining how to read a bank statement."
Who is it for and what do they already know?
"For women traders in Jos who use a phone banking app but find statements confusing."
What shape should the answer take?
"Use a short intro, 5 numbered steps and a 3-question self-check."
What must it avoid or include?
"Simple English, under 350 words, no invented bank names or fees."

blocks.text: Compare the difference. A weak prompt says: "Write a handout on bank statements." The result is usually a long, generic page aimed at nobody in particular, with words like "reconciliation" left unexplained. The strong prompt in the table above tells the model who the readers are, what they already know, how long it should be and what to avoid, so the first draft is already close to usable and needs only checking and small edits.
You do not need all five every time, but the more the task matters, the more parts you should include. Writing the prompt in your phone notes first, then pasting it, helps you think it through.
The workflow

blocks.title: Prompt, draft, check, edit
items: Define the task
Prompt with context
Review the draft
Check facts and numbers
Edit and own it
blocks.caption: If the review shows big problems, go round again with a better prompt rather than patching a weak draft.

items: **Define**: write one sentence on what the finished work must achieve and who will use it.
**Prompt**: use the five parts, and paste any source text the answer should be based on.
**Review**: read the whole draft. Does it answer the task? Is the tone right for the audience?
**Check**: verify every name, date, number and claim (Lesson 2.3 shows how).
**Edit and own**: rewrite in your voice, add what only you know, and remove anything you cannot confirm.

blocks.text: Improving a weak answer
The first answer is a starting point. Instead of starting again, tell the model exactly what to change. Useful follow-ups:

items: "Make it simpler: short sentences, no jargon, as if for someone who left school after primary."
"Cut it to half the length and keep the steps."
"Give me three different openings so I can choose."
"What questions should I answer to make this more accurate for my situation?"
"List any facts in your answer that I should check before using it."

blocks.title: Worked example: a meeting summary from rough notes
blocks.context: For example, Ruth is secretary of a women's association in Calabar. After a 2-hour meeting she has 400 words of rough notes and must send minutes to 35 members by evening.
steps: Define: "Clear minutes that record decisions, who will act, and deadlines, readable on WhatsApp."

Prompt: "Act as an experienced association secretary. Turn the notes below into minutes for 35 members. Format: date, attendance, 4 to 6 decisions as numbered points, an action table with person and deadline. Use only what is in the notes; write NOT STATED where something is missing. Under 300 words." She pastes the notes with members' surnames replaced by initials.
Review: the draft is clear but lists a deadline of "30 June" for the hall booking. Her notes said "end of the month".
Check: she asks the treasurer and confirms the real deadline is 28 June, then corrects it. She also sees the AI wrote attendance as 30; her notes say 27, so she fixes it.
Edit: she puts back members' full names, adds a line thanking the hosts, and sends.
blocks.result: Ruth finishes in about 25 minutes instead of over an hour, and two errors the AI introduced (a guessed date and a wrong attendance figure) were caught because she checked against her notes.

blocks.title: Use NOT STATED
blocks.text: Telling the model to write NOT STATED, or similar, when information is missing makes it far less likely to fill gaps with guesses, and shows you exactly what to find out.
When to stop prompting

If three rounds of follow-ups have not fixed the draft, the problem is usually that the model lacks information only you have. Stop, write that section yourself, and use AI only for tidying. Also stop when the task is personal: a condolence message or an apology to a colleague should sound like you, not a template.

blocks.title: Say when AI helped
blocks.text: In many workplaces and schools it is now expected that you say when AI helped produce work. A simple line such as "Drafted with AI assistance and checked by Ruth O." builds trust. Follow your organisation's rules.
This workflow works for letters, handouts, lesson plans, proposals and reports alike. The quality comes from your definition, your context and your checking, not from any secret prompt.

takeaways: A clear prompt covers role, task, context, format and limits.
Use the cycle: define, prompt, review, check, edit and own.
Ask for NOT STATED instead of guesses when information is missing.
After three weak rounds, write the hard part yourself.

activity.title: Run the full workflow once
steps: Choose a real document you must produce this week (minutes, a letter, a handout or a report).
Write your one-sentence definition of done.
Write a five-part prompt and paste in any anonymised source notes.
Use at least two follow-up prompts to improve the draft.
Check every fact and number against your source, then edit it into your own voice.
Note how long each stage took.
activity.evidence: Your prompt, the first AI draft, your final version with changes highlighted, and your stage timings

lessons.title: Checking AI answers: facts, sums, sources and bias
objectives: Apply the SIFT method to verify a claim from an AI answer
Recalculate figures in AI output and catch arithmetic errors
Spot signs of bias or stereotype in AI-generated text and images
Keep a check record that shows what you verified and changed

blocks.text: Checking is the skill that separates an AI-literate professional from a casual user. Anyone can get a fluent answer. Your value is knowing which parts to trust and proving the rest.

blocks.name: verify-data
blocks.alt: A person checking data against a list
blocks.caption: Every fact, figure and source in AI output needs checking before it is shared.

blocks.text: What to check, in order

items: **Numbers**: totals, percentages, dates, prices, quantities.
**Names and titles**: people, organisations, laws, agencies, books.
**Sources and links**: does the reference exist, and does it say what the AI claims?
**Instructions**: steps on official processes, such as registering a business or applying for a grant.
**Tone and fairness**: does it stereotype any group of people?

blocks.text: The SIFT method for facts
SIFT is a fact-checking method developed by digital literacy educator Mike Caulfield. It was designed for web content and works well for AI answers.

blocks.title: SIFT: four moves
items: Stop
Investigate the source
Find better coverage
Trace to the original
blocks.caption: Pause before trusting a claim, then confirm it from reliable, original sources.

head: Move
What you do with an AI claim
rows: Notice a specific claim (a fee, a date, a statistic) and do not share it yet
If the AI gave a link, open it. Is it a real, official or reputable site?
Search the claim yourself and see what official or trusted sources say
Go to the first source: the agency's website, the law itself, the original report

blocks.title: Worked example: correcting an AI answer with wrong figures
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma runs a tailoring business in Onitsha. She asked a chatbot to work out her profit margin and it replied: "You sold 40 gowns at 18,000 naira each and spent 450,000 naira on materials and labour, so your profit is 270,000 naira, a margin of 60%."
steps: Stop: two numbers to check, the profit and the margin.
Revenue: 40 x 18,000 = 720,000 naira.
Profit: 720,000 - 450,000 = 270,000 naira. The AI is right here.
Margin: profit divided by revenue, 270,000 / 720,000 = 0.375, which is 37.5%.
The AI's 60% is wrong. It divided profit by costs (270,000 / 450,000 = 0.6), which is a different measure called markup on cost.
She records the error and the correct figure in her check record.
blocks.result: Profit is 270,000 naira and the profit margin is 37.5%, not 60%. Had she used the AI figure, she might have cut prices thinking she had more room than she does.

blocks.title: Use a calculator, not the chatbot
blocks.text: For any sum that matters, redo it on your phone calculator or in a spreadsheet. Ask the AI to show each step so you can see exactly where it went wrong.
Checking sources

If a chatbot cites a book, article or law, search for the exact title. Common problems: the title does not exist; it exists but by a different author; or it exists but does not say what the AI claimed. For Nigerian processes, trace to the official site, for example cac.gov.ng for business registration, ndpc.gov.ng for data protection, or nafdac.gov.ng for product registration.
Checking images and screenshots

AI can now produce realistic photos, flyers and screenshots. Before you forward a striking image or a "screenshot" of an announcement, look closely: hands with odd fingers, writing that turns into nonsense, logos slightly wrong, or lighting that does not match. Use **Google Lens** (search with an image) to see where else the picture has appeared and when. For announcements about grants, jobs or payments, go to the organisation's official website or verified social media page. If you cannot confirm it, do not share it, even with a warning.
Bias and stereotypes

Because AI learns from human data, it can repeat human bias. Image tools asked for "a CEO" may show mostly men; text tools may assume a nurse is a woman and an engineer is a man, or describe African countries mainly through poverty. Research by Joy Buolamwini and others has shown that some face analysis systems performed worse on darker-skinned women than on lighter-skinned men.

items: Read AI text and ask: would this sound fair if it described my own community?
When generating images of people, state who you want to see, for example "a Nigerian woman engineer at work".
Never use AI alone to rank, select or reject people for jobs, loans, admissions or support.

blocks.text: Your check record
A check record is a simple table, in a notebook or spreadsheet, that proves what you verified. It protects you if work is questioned and it shows you which tasks the AI gets wrong most often.

blocks.title: When you cannot verify, remove it
blocks.text: If you cannot confirm a figure, name or reference from a reliable source, take it out or clearly mark it as unconfirmed. Never pass on an unchecked AI claim as fact.

takeaways: Check numbers, names, sources, instructions and fairness, in that order.
SIFT: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace to the original.
Redo important sums yourself; margin is profit divided by revenue.
AI can repeat bias; never let it alone decide about people.
Keep a check record and remove anything you cannot verify.

activity.title: Check and correct one AI answer
steps: Ask a chatbot a question in your field that includes at least two facts and one calculation.
List every checkable claim in the answer.
Verify each claim with SIFT and recalculate the numbers yourself.
Record each check in a check record table with five columns as shown.
Write a corrected version of the answer.
activity.evidence: The original AI answer, your completed check record, and your corrected version

quiz.q: Blessing wants AI help replying to a member's complaint that includes the member's phone number and home address. What should she do first?
options: Paste it as it is; the chatbot keeps it private
Remove the phone number and address and replace the name before pasting
Send it to Meta AI because it is inside WhatsApp
Ask the member for permission to share her bank details too
quiz.explain: Anonymise first. The AI does not need personal contact details to draft a reply, and you are responsible for protecting that data.

quiz.q: Which prompt is most likely to give a useful handout?
options: "Write about saving money."
"Write a really good handout, please."
"Act as a financial literacy trainer. Write a one-page handout on starting a savings habit for market women in Aba, with 5 numbered steps, under 300 words, simple English, no invented bank names."
"Saving money handout Nigeria women long."
quiz.explain: It includes role, task, context, format and limits, so the model has what it needs.

quiz.q: A chatbot says: revenue 500,000 naira, costs 400,000 naira, profit margin 25%. What is the correct profit margin?
quiz.explain: Profit is 500,000 - 400,000 = 100,000. Margin is 100,000 / 500,000 = 20%. The 25% is profit divided by costs, which is markup.

quiz.q: In the SIFT method, what does "Trace to the original" mean for an AI claim about a CAC fee?
options: Ask the chatbot again to confirm
Find the figure on the official CAC website or from the CAC office
Search social media for what others paid
Use the figure if two blogs agree
quiz.explain: Tracing means going to the first, authoritative source, which for a CAC fee is CAC itself.

quiz.q: After three rounds of follow-up prompts, Ruth's draft still gets key details of her project wrong. What is the best next step?
options: Keep prompting until it is right
Switch to a paid plan
Write that section herself, then use AI only to tidy it
Send it anyway with a note that AI wrote it
quiz.explain: Repeated errors usually mean the model lacks information only she has. She should write it herself and use AI for polishing.

modules.title: Leading Responsible AI Use
modules.overview: You will learn to help a team, school, cooperative or client use AI well: finding the tasks where it truly helps, costing and scoping AI training or support, and writing a short AI use policy. You will finish with a portfolio of evidence that shows your critical AI skills.

lessons.title: Discovery: finding where AI genuinely helps a team
objectives: Run a discovery conversation using structured questions
Build a task inventory and score each task for value and risk
Recommend which tasks to start with, which to delay and which to keep human
Recognise when AI is not the answer

blocks.text: When a school, NGO or small business asks "How can we use AI?", the wrong response is to start with tools. The right response is to start with their work. **Discovery** means understanding what people actually do each week, what slows them down, and what would go wrong if a mistake slipped through.

blocks.name: questions
blocks.alt: A person surrounded by question marks
blocks.caption: Good AI advice starts with questions about the work, not with a list of tools.

blocks.text: Discovery questions
Ask these in a short meeting or by voice note, and write the answers down in their words.

items: Which written or repeated tasks take the most time each week?
Who reads the result, and what happens if it contains a mistake?
Does the task involve personal data about members, students, patients or clients?
Are staff already using AI tools? Which ones, and for what?
What devices and data budget do staff have?
Are there rules from funders, regulators or the board about data or AI?
What would success look like in three months?

blocks.title: Ask about current use
blocks.text: In many organisations some staff already use chatbots quietly, sometimes with sensitive data. Asking openly, without blame, gives you the real starting point.
Running the discovery meeting

items: Agree the time and who will attend: ideally the leader plus two or three people who do the daily work.
Explain the purpose in one sentence: "I want to understand your work so any AI advice fits you."
Ask the questions one at a time and let people give examples. Ask "Can you show me?" when they mention a document.
Write down tasks exactly as people describe them, with how often they happen and how long they take.
Close by reading back the main tasks and asking: "Did I miss anything important?"
Send a short thank-you message and say when they will receive your summary.

blocks.text: Listen more than you speak. Staff who do the work often know exactly where time is wasted, and they are the people who will have to use, or resist, whatever you recommend.
Build a task inventory

List every task mentioned, then score each on two scales from 1 to 5. **Value**: how much time AI could save, or how much quality it could add (5 is most). **Risk**: how much harm a mistake or data leak would cause (5 is most). Then plot each task.

blocks.title: Value and risk map
items: Start here
Pilot with safeguards
Low priority
Keep human-led
blocks.caption: High value and low risk tasks are the best first projects; high risk tasks stay with people, whatever their value.

blocks.title: Worked example: discovery for a private secondary school
blocks.context: For example, Mrs Okon owns a secondary school in Uyo with 14 teachers. She asks Chioma, an AI literacy graduate, for advice. Chioma interviews her and three teachers and scores six tasks.
steps: Lesson note first drafts: value 5, risk 2. Start here, with teacher review.
Practice quiz questions from the scheme of work: value 4, risk 2. Start here.
Newsletter to parents: value 3, risk 2. Start here, head teacher approves.
Report card comments on each student: value 4, risk 4. Pilot only, with teachers writing from their own notes and no names pasted in.
Deciding which students repeat a class: value 2, risk 5. Keep human-led; no AI.
Answering parents' fee questions automatically: value 3, risk 4. Delay; wrong answers about money damage trust.
blocks.result: Chioma recommends three starting tasks, one careful pilot, one delayed task and one task that stays fully human. Her advice is specific to the school and defensible to parents.

blocks.text: When AI is not the answer

Discovery often reveals problems AI cannot fix. If reports take long because nobody has the data, the fix is a better record-keeping habit. If staff miss deadlines because of unclear roles, the fix is management. Saying "AI will not help here, but this will" builds more trust than selling a tool.

items: Missing or messy information: fix records first.
Tasks needing care and relationships, such as counselling or resolving a conflict.
Decisions about people's rights, money or safety.
Very small volumes: if a task happens twice a year, training people on AI for it may cost more than it saves.

blocks.title: Watch for data in the inventory
blocks.text: Mark every task that touches personal data. These need anonymisation rules, consent where required under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, and a named person accountable.
Writing up your findings
Summarise discovery on one page: the tasks, their scores, your recommendation for each, the data cautions, and two or three next steps. Keep it short enough that a busy owner reads it the same day.

head: Section of summary
What Chioma wrote for the school
rows: Six tasks, scored for value and risk with teachers
Lesson note drafts, practice questions, parents' newsletter
Report card comments, no student names pasted in
Fee questions delayed; repeat-class decisions stay with staff
No student names, results or family details in any AI tool
Safe setup session for all 14 teachers; review the pilot after four weeks

takeaways: Start with the work, not the tools.
Score each task for value and risk, then plot it.
High-risk decisions about people stay human-led.
Sometimes the honest finding is that AI is not the fix.

activity.title: Run a mini discovery
steps: Choose a real group: your workplace team, a cooperative, a church committee or a small business.
Ask at least five of the discovery questions and write down the answers.
List at least six tasks and score each for value and risk from 1 to 5.
Place them on the value and risk map.
Write a one-page summary with a recommendation for each task.
activity.evidence: Your interview notes, the scored task table, and your one-page summary

lessons.title: Costing, proposals and scope for AI literacy support
objectives: Cost an AI literacy workshop or support package from your real expenses
Write a short proposal with clear deliverables and exclusions
Control scope when a client asks for more than was agreed
Set honest expectations about what AI training can achieve

blocks.text: Once you can use AI critically, others will ask for help: a cooperative wanting a training day, an NGO wanting staff guidance, a school wanting a policy. Whether you do this as paid work or as a volunteer, you need a clear cost, a clear proposal and clear limits.

blocks.name: contract
blocks.alt: A person reviewing a contract document
blocks.caption: A written proposal with clear limits protects both you and the group you serve.

blocks.text: Cost before you price
List every cost, including your time. Then decide your price or, if volunteering, what support you need to cover expenses.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing a one-day workshop
blocks.context: For example, Folake is asked by a market women's association in Abeokuta to run a one-day "Using AI safely on your phone" workshop for 20 members. All figures are approximate and for illustration; use your own local prices.
steps: Preparation: 6 hours. Delivery: 6 hours. Follow-up support on WhatsApp: 2 hours. Total time: 14 hours.
She values her time at 5,000 naira an hour (her choice): 14 x 5,000 = 70,000 naira.
Printing a 4-page handout for 20 people at about 100 naira a page: 20 x 4 x 100 = 8,000 naira.
Transport there and back: about 6,000 naira.
Data for demonstrations: about 3,000 naira.
Direct costs: 8,000 + 6,000 + 3,000 = 17,000 naira. Total cost including time: 70,000 + 17,000 = 87,000 naira.
Cost per participant: 87,000 / 20 = 4,350 naira.
blocks.result: Folake quotes 90,000 naira for the day (about 4,500 naira per member), which covers her costs. If the association cannot pay, she knows exactly what support to ask a sponsor for.

blocks.title: Volunteering still needs costing
blocks.text: Even unpaid work has costs. Knowing that a workshop costs about 17,000 naira in direct expenses lets you ask a sponsor or the association to cover them, so helping others does not drain your own pocket.
Packages you could offer

head: Package
What it includes
Good for
rows: 2 hours: install, privacy settings, two-step verification, no-paste list
One day: prompting, checking, three real tasks from the group's own work
Interviews, value and risk map, one-page policy, one review meeting
A fixed number of weeks of WhatsApp questions with set response times

blocks.text: Fixed packages are easier to price and explain than open-ended hourly help. They also make scope clear from the start.
What goes in a short proposal

head: Section
What to write
rows: One sentence: what the group will be able to do after your support
Exactly what you provide: sessions, hours, handouts, follow-up period
What you will not do, for example paying for anyone's AI subscription, handling members' personal data, or giving legal advice
What the group provides: venue, phones charged, attendance list, a contact person
Dates for preparation, delivery and follow-up
Amount, what it covers, when it is paid, and how (bank transfer, Moniepoint, OPay or similar)
How success will be judged, for example each member completes a safe setup checklist

blocks.text: Controlling scope

**Scope creep** is when the work quietly grows beyond what was agreed: "Since you are here, can you also set up our Facebook page and write our grant?" Each request seems small, but together they can double your time.

blocks.title: Handling a new request
items: Hear the request
Check the proposal
In scope: do it
Out of scope: quote separately
Confirm in writing
blocks.caption: Every new request is checked against the written agreement before you say yes.

items: Thank them for the request and say you will check what was agreed.
Compare it with the deliverables and exclusions in your proposal.
If it is included, do it. If not, explain kindly and offer a separate price or a later date.
Confirm any change by WhatsApp message or email so both sides have a record.

blocks.text: Honest expectations

Do not promise that AI will "double productivity" or "replace staff". You cannot verify such claims for a specific group. Promise what you can measure: participants will set up a tool safely, write a clear prompt, and check an answer. If you measured time savings in earlier lessons, share those real figures and how you got them.
Measuring the outcome

Build a simple check into every package so both sides can see what was achieved. At the start, ask each participant to rate their confidence from 1 to 5 on three skills: setting up a tool safely, writing a clear prompt, and checking an answer. Ask again at the end, and once more after a month. Also count practical results: how many completed the safe setup checklist, and how many produced one checked piece of real work. Report these numbers honestly in a short follow-up message, including what did not go well and what you will change next time.

blocks.title: Payment safety
blocks.text: Agree payment in writing, take payment by traceable bank transfer, and confirm money has arrived in your account app before treating it as paid. Screenshots of transfers can be faked.

takeaways: Cost your time and every direct expense before setting a price.
A proposal states deliverables, exclusions, responsibilities, timeline and payment.
Check every new request against the agreement and confirm changes in writing.
Promise measurable skills, not general claims about AI.

activity.title: Cost and propose one support package
steps: Pick a realistic group you could help with AI literacy.
Estimate your hours for preparation, delivery and follow-up, and list direct costs with local approximate prices.
Calculate total cost and cost per participant.
Write a one-page proposal using the seven sections in this lesson.
Write a polite two-sentence reply to an out-of-scope request.
activity.evidence: Your costing sheet with calculations, your one-page proposal, and your scope reply

lessons.title: Writing an AI use policy, leading others and building your portfolio
objectives: Draft a one-page AI use policy for a team or organisation
Introduce AI to colleagues in stages that build safe habits
Assemble a portfolio showing critical AI use with evidence
Plan your next 90 days as an AI-literate leader

blocks.text: Teams that use AI without agreed rules end up with uneven quality, leaked data and confusion about who is responsible. A short, clear **AI use policy** solves this. It does not need lawyers' language. It needs plain rules people can follow on their phones.

blocks.name: team-collaboration
blocks.alt: A team working together around a shared board
blocks.caption: A short shared policy lets a whole team use AI the same safe way.

blocks.text: Seven parts of a one-page policy

head: Part
Example wording
rows: "We use AI to save time on drafting and summarising, while protecting the people we serve."
"Staff may use the free versions of ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot from the official apps."
"First drafts, rewriting, summaries of non-confidential documents, idea lists, training materials."
"Decisions about hiring, discipline, admissions or support; medical or legal advice; creating images or audio of real people without consent."
"No names, phone numbers, ID numbers, bank details or health information of members or clients. Anonymise first."
"A named person checks every fact and figure before anything is sent outside the team."
"We say when AI helped with published work. This policy is reviewed every six months."

blocks.text: Base your rules on recognised principles: UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI stresses human oversight, fairness, transparency and privacy; the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets the legal baseline for personal data. Where your organisation has funders or regulators, check their rules too.

blocks.title: Deepfakes and consent
blocks.text: Never create or share AI images, video or voice of a real person without their clear permission, and never use AI to make anyone appear to say or do something they did not. This can cause serious harm and may break the law.
When the policy is broken
Sooner or later someone will paste personal data into a chatbot or send out an AI error. Respond calmly and quickly, because the aim is to limit harm and learn, not to shame.

items: Find out exactly what happened: which tool, what data or error, and who received it.
Limit the harm: delete the chat, correct the message, and tell anyone who received wrong information.
If other people's personal data was exposed, tell the person responsible for data protection in your organisation, who will judge whether the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 requires further steps.
Agree what will prevent a repeat, such as a reminder session or a clearer rule.
Record the incident and the fix, and use it at the next policy review.

blocks.text: Leading others in stages

blocks.title: Introducing AI to a team
items: Week 1: safe setup
Weeks 2-3: one pilot task
Week 4: review results
Month 2: policy agreed
Month 3: expand carefully
blocks.caption: Small steps with a review point build good habits before AI spreads to riskier work.

items: **Start with safety**: everyone completes the safe setup checklist from Lesson 2.1.
**Pilot one low-risk task** from your discovery map, such as meeting minutes.
**Review together**: what errors did AI make, and what did checking catch?
**Agree the policy** using what the pilot taught you.
**Expand slowly**, adding tasks one at a time and keeping the check record.

blocks.text: Expect mixed feelings. Some colleagues fear AI will replace them; others trust it too much. Address both: show that the human checking step is essential, and show real examples of AI errors caught in your pilot.
Your portfolio
Employers and clients cannot see your judgement unless you show it. A strong AI literacy portfolio holds a few well-documented cases rather than many screenshots.

blocks.title: Worked example: one portfolio case
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi works in the admin office of a health NGO in Enugu and is building her portfolio.
steps: Task: summarise a 20-page donor report into a 1-page brief for the board.
Prompt: she records her five-part prompt and notes that she removed all patient details first.
Check: her check record shows 9 figures verified; 2 were wrong (a total of 1,240 that should have been 1,420, and a date in the wrong year). Both corrected.
Edit: she shows the AI draft and her final brief side by side with changes highlighted.
Result: she timed the work at 50 minutes compared with about 2 hours before, and the board accepted the brief.
blocks.result: One clear case shows prompting, data protection, fact-checking, editing and a measured result: exactly the skills an employer wants to see.

items: Collect three cases of AI use in your own work, each with prompt, draft, check record and final version.
Include at least one case where you found and corrected an AI error.
Add your one-page AI use policy or discovery summary.
Write a short reflection on the ethical points that matter most in your setting.
Store it in Google Drive or a similar folder with personal data removed, ready to share as a link.

blocks.title: Keep learning
blocks.text: AI tools change every few months. Set a reminder to review your policy, settings and check habits every quarter, and re-test one old task with the newest version of your tool.

takeaways: A one-page policy covers purpose, tools, allowed uses, banned uses, data rules, human review and disclosure.
Introduce AI in stages: safe setup, pilot, review, policy, expand.
Never create AI media of real people without consent.
A portfolio of a few documented cases proves your critical skill.

activity.title: Draft your policy and first portfolio case
steps: Write a one-page AI use policy for your team, cooperative or business using the seven parts.
Ask one colleague or fellow member to read it and suggest one change.
Choose one task from earlier activities and write it up as a portfolio case with all five elements.
Write a 90-day plan with one action per month.
activity.evidence: Your one-page policy with the reviewer's comment, one complete portfolio case, and your 90-day plan

quiz.q: A school owner asks Chioma which AI tool to buy for her staff. What should Chioma do first?
options: Recommend the most popular paid tool
Ask discovery questions about the staff's tasks, risks and data
Install Meta AI on every teacher's phone
Tell her AI is not suitable for schools
quiz.explain: Discovery comes before tools. The right tool and tasks depend on the work, the risks and the data involved.

quiz.q: Which task should stay human-led even if AI could save time?
options: Drafting a parents' newsletter
Writing practice quiz questions
Deciding which students must repeat a class
Summarising a non-confidential training report
quiz.explain: Decisions about people's rights and futures are high risk and must stay with accountable humans.

quiz.q: Folake's workshop costs 18,000 naira in direct expenses and 12 hours of her time valued at 4,000 naira an hour. There are 15 participants. What is the total cost per participant?
options: 1,200 naira
3,200 naira
4,400 naira
4,000 naira
quiz.explain: Time: 12 x 4,000 = 48,000 naira. Total: 48,000 + 18,000 = 66,000 naira. Per participant: 66,000 / 15 = 4,400 naira. 1,200 naira counts only the expenses.

quiz.q: Midway through a workshop, the association asks Folake to also write their grant application. What is the best response?
options: Agree immediately to keep them happy
Refuse to talk about it
Check the proposal, explain it is outside the agreed scope, and offer a separate quote or date in writing
Ask a chatbot to write the grant during the workshop
quiz.explain: New requests are checked against the agreement. Out-of-scope work gets a separate quote, confirmed in writing.

quiz.q: Which line belongs in the data rules of an AI use policy?
options: "Staff may use AI for first drafts."
"No names, phone numbers, ID numbers or health details of clients may be pasted into AI tools."
"This policy is reviewed every six months."
"We use AI to save time on drafting."
quiz.explain: Data rules say what information must not go into AI tools. The others belong to allowed uses, review, and purpose.

finalQuiz.q: Which statement best describes how a chatbot such as ChatGPT produces an answer?
options: It searches a database of verified answers
It predicts the next piece of text again and again
It copies the top Google result
A human writes each reply in real time
finalQuiz.explain: An LLM generates text by repeated next-token prediction, which is why it can sound right while being wrong.

finalQuiz.q: On the reliability and risk grid, where does "telling a member the dose of a medicine" belong?
options: Use freely, light check
Use, then check every fact
Use with care, human decides
Avoid AI; use a qualified health worker
finalQuiz.explain: Medicine questions are high harm and AI is unreliable for them. Refer to a qualified health worker.

finalQuiz.q: Roughly how many tokens is a 750-word English text, using 100 tokens for about 75 words?
options: About 560
About 750
About 1,000
About 3,000

finalQuiz.q: Why should a fluent speaker check an AI translation into Hausa before it is sent to members?
options: AI tools refuse to translate Hausa
Chatbots learned far less from Hausa text, so errors in meaning are more likely
Hausa translations use too much data
It is required by NAFDAC
finalQuiz.explain: Most training text is English. African languages have less online text, so translation quality is lower.

finalQuiz.q: A report takes 100 minutes by hand. With AI it takes 30 minutes to draft and 25 minutes to check. How many minutes are saved over 6 reports?
finalQuiz.explain: With AI: 30 + 25 = 55 minutes. Saving per report: 100 - 55 = 45. Over 6 reports: 45 x 6 = 270 minutes.

finalQuiz.q: Which of these is safe to paste into a chatbot?
options: A member's BVN to check a loan form
A client's full name and home address
An anonymised summary of a meeting with names replaced by roles
A one-time code from your bank
finalQuiz.explain: Anonymised text is fine. ID numbers, addresses and codes must never go into a chatbot.

finalQuiz.q: Which part of a prompt is "Simple English, under 300 words, no invented fees"?
options: Role
Context
Format
Limits
finalQuiz.explain: Limits say what the answer must avoid or stay within.

finalQuiz.q: An AI says revenue is 600,000 naira, costs 450,000 naira, so the margin is 33%. What is the correct margin?
finalQuiz.explain: Profit is 150,000. Margin is 150,000 / 600,000 = 25%. 33% is profit divided by costs (markup).

finalQuiz.q: A chatbot cites "Section 14 of the Nigerian Small Traders Act". What should you do?
options: Use it, because AI rarely invents laws
Ask the chatbot if it is sure
Search for the law and trace it to an official source before using it
Remove only the section number
finalQuiz.explain: Laws and references are often hallucinated. Trace the claim to the original source; if you cannot find it, remove it.

finalQuiz.q: A cooperative wants AI to choose which members receive a loan. What is the right advice?
options: Use AI to rank members to save time
Use AI, but only for members with smartphones
Keep the decision with accountable people; AI may help only with admin like drafting letters
Use two AI tools and compare the rankings
finalQuiz.explain: Decisions about people's money and rights are high risk and must stay human-led.

finalQuiz.q: In the costing lesson, what is the main reason to cost a workshop you are giving for free?
options: To charge members later
To know exactly what expenses to ask a sponsor or host to cover
Because CAC requires it
To make the proposal longer
finalQuiz.explain: Costing shows the real expenses, so volunteering does not drain your own money.

finalQuiz.q: Which is the best first step when introducing AI to a whole team?
options: Allow everyone to use any AI app for any task
Everyone completes a safe setup checklist, then the team pilots one low-risk task
Start with automated replies to clients about fees
Ban AI completely
finalQuiz.explain: Stage it: safe setup, a low-risk pilot, review, then an agreed policy before expanding.

capstone.title: Critical AI Literacy Application Project
capstone.brief: Document three real uses of AI in your own work with your prompts, drafts, check records and edited final versions; show one case where you found and corrected an inaccurate or incomplete AI answer; and write a one-page AI use policy with a short reflection on the ethics that matter in your context.
steps: Map at least eight of your tasks on the reliability and risk grid and choose three suitable for AI.
Set up one AI tool safely and record your privacy and security settings.
Complete each of the three tasks using the prompt, draft, check, edit workflow, timing each stage.
Keep a check record for each task, verifying every fact and figure with SIFT and your own calculations.
Write up the case where you corrected an AI error: the original claim, how you checked it, and the corrected version.
Draft a one-page AI use policy for your team or organisation and get one person's feedback.
Write a 300-word reflection on data protection, fairness and human oversight in your setting, and assemble everything in one shared folder.
evidence: Screenshots of safe settings with personal details hidden
Three documented cases: prompt, AI draft, check record, final version, timings
One error-correction case with the source used to verify it
One-page AI use policy with reviewer comment
No personal data of others anywhere in the folder
